hazard-risk-and-risk-control-in-theatre.title: Hazard, risk and risk control
hazard-risk-and-risk-control-in-theatre.caption: Five core terms of occupational safety and health.
hazard-risk-and-risk-control-in-theatre.body:
In short: Five core terms of occupational safety and health.

Hazard, risk and risk control

  1. Hazard. Anything that could cause harm: a thing, a condition or a behaviour. A wet floor or a sharp blade.
  2. Hazard identification. Walking through each work area and task to spot the hazards in the job.
  3. Risk. The chance that harm will actually happen when someone meets the hazard.
  4. Risk control. Acting to remove or reduce the risk as far as is reasonably practicable.
  5. Monitoring and review. Checking again that the controls still work and changing them if they do not.

Why it matters in theatre

Theatre is full of hazards: sharps, diathermy, cleaning chemicals, lifting and blood or body fluids. Knowing the words helps you report problems clearly.

Remember

A hazard is the danger. Risk is the chance it hurts someone.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Hazard, risk and risk control".

Hazard: Anything that could cause harm: a thing, a condition or a behaviour. A wet floor or a sharp blade; Hazard identification: Walking through each work area and task to spot the hazards in the job; Risk: The chance that harm will actually happen when someone meets the hazard; Risk control: Acting to remove or reduce the risk as far as is reasonably practicable; Monitoring and review: Checking again that the controls still work and changing them if they do not.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

Based on TVET CDACC, Learning Guide for Basic Competencies Level 6 (2019), rewritten as short study notes.

six-types-of-hazard-in-the-operating-the.title: Six types of workplace hazard
six-types-of-hazard-in-the-operating-the.caption: The guide groups hazards into six types.
six-types-of-hazard-in-the-operating-the.body:
In short: The guide groups hazards into six types.

Six types of workplace hazard

  1. Safety hazards. Spills, clutter, poor storage, electrical faults, gas leaks, falling objects.
  2. Unsafe behaviour. Smoking in banned areas, alcohol or drug use at work, rushing and shortcuts.
  3. Physical hazards. Noise, heat, poor lighting, vibration, pressure and radiation.
  4. Ergonomic and stress hazards. Heavy lifting, long standing, fatigue, pressure and long hours.
  5. Chemical hazards. Dust, fumes, gases and vapours, such as disinfectants and anaesthetic gases.
  6. Biological hazards. Bacteria, viruses, fungi and other organisms, including blood and body fluids.

Why it matters in theatre

In theatre these show up as wet floors, noisy equipment, long cases, cleaning chemicals and infected material.

Remember

Check each hazard type every time you set up a theatre.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Six types of workplace hazard".

Safety hazards: Spills, clutter, poor storage, electrical faults, gas leaks, falling objects; Unsafe behaviour: Smoking in banned areas, alcohol or drug use at work, rushing and shortcuts; Physical hazards: Noise, heat, poor lighting, vibration, pressure and radiation; Ergonomic and stress hazards: Heavy lifting, long standing, fatigue, pressure and long hours; Chemical hazards: Dust, fumes, gases and vapours, such as disinfectants and anaesthetic gases; Biological hazards: Bacteria, viruses, fungi and other organisms, including blood and body fluids.

signs-that-a-workplace-has-a-hazard-prob.title: Warning signs of a hazard problem
signs-that-a-workplace-has-a-hazard-prob.caption: Four indicators that hazards are present.
signs-that-a-workplace-has-a-hazard-prob.body:
In short: Four indicators that hazards are present.

Warning signs of a hazard problem

  1. More accidents and injuries. A rising number of incidents is the clearest sign something is wrong.
  2. More sickness. Staff report illness, symptoms or health complaints linked to the work.
  3. Repeated worker complaints. The same safety or health concerns keep being raised.
  4. High absenteeism. Staff stay away for reasons connected to the work.

Why it matters in theatre

Reporting early patterns, such as repeated needle-stick injuries or back pain in the team, lets the hospital act before someone is seriously hurt.

Remember

Listen when colleagues complain. It is often the first warning.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Warning signs of a hazard problem".

More accidents and injuries: A rising number of incidents is the clearest sign something is wrong; More sickness: Staff report illness, symptoms or health complaints linked to the work; Repeated worker complaints: The same safety or health concerns keep being raised; High absenteeism: Staff stay away for reasons connected to the work.

how-workplace-hazards-are-checked-and-re.title: Checking the workplace for hazards
how-workplace-hazards-are-checked-and-re.caption: Audits and worker feedback show where the hazards are.
how-workplace-hazards-are-checked-and-re.body:
In short: Audits and worker feedback show where the hazards are.

Checking the workplace for hazards

  1. Health audit. Health professionals check how worker care measures up against set standards.
  2. Safety audit. A structured review of how well the safety and health system works.
  3. Questionnaires. Ask staff in writing about hazards and worries.
  4. Oral interviews. Talk to workers about what they see and experience.
  5. Suggestion box. Lets staff raise concerns without being identified.
  6. Act on the results. Analyse what is collected and take corrective action.

Why it matters in theatre

Theatre staff know best where the risks are. Their reports feed the safety audit.

Remember

Workers see hazards first. Ask them, then act.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Checking the workplace for hazards".

Health audit: Health professionals check how worker care measures up against set standards; Safety audit: A structured review of how well the safety and health system works; Questionnaires: Ask staff in writing about hazards and worries; Oral interviews: Talk to workers about what they see and experience; Suggestion box: Lets staff raise concerns without being identified; Act on the results: Analyse what is collected and take corrective action.

hierarchy-of-hazard-controls-with-theatr.title: Six ways to control a hazard
hierarchy-of-hazard-controls-with-theatr.caption: The six control measures, strongest first.
hierarchy-of-hazard-controls-with-theatr.body:
In short: The six control measures, strongest first.

Six ways to control a hazard

  1. Elimination. Remove the hazard completely: clear trip hazards, dispose of unwanted chemicals.
  2. Substitution. Replace it with something safer, such as a safer chemical or a quieter machine.
  3. Isolation. Separate people from it with distance or barriers, such as a fume cabinet.
  4. Engineering controls. Use a physical fix: machine guards, good ventilation, fair work rosters.
  5. Administrative controls. Safe procedures, training, warning signs, shorter exposure, good housekeeping.
  6. Protective equipment (PPE). Gloves, masks, eyewear, aprons. The last line of protection.

Why it matters in theatre

PPE protects only if it is worn correctly, so remove or reduce the hazard first wherever you can.

Remember

Try to remove the hazard first. PPE is the last defence.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Six ways to control a hazard".

The last line of protection.

personal-protective-equipment-ppe-in-the.title: PPE: the last line of protection
personal-protective-equipment-ppe-in-the.caption: PPE items listed in the guide, and how they fit into theatre work.
personal-protective-equipment-ppe-in-the.body:
In short: PPE items listed in the guide, and how they fit into theatre work.

PPE: the last line of protection

  1. Gloves. Protect hands from chemicals and body fluids.
  2. Face mask. Protects the nose and mouth from splashes and airborne particles.
  3. Protective eyewear. Shields the eyes from splashes and flying particles.
  4. Apron. Keeps fluids and chemicals off clothing and skin.
  5. Ear plugs. Protect hearing around loud machinery.
  6. Fit and care. Train staff to wear it correctly. Keep it clean and in good repair.

Why it matters in theatre

Choose PPE to match the hazard and the job. Follow your hospital policy for each procedure.

Remember

PPE only protects when you wear it properly every time.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "PPE: the last line of protection".

Gloves: Protect hands from chemicals and body fluids; Face mask: Protects the nose and mouth from splashes and airborne particles; Protective eyewear: Shields the eyes from splashes and flying particles; Apron: Keeps fluids and chemicals off clothing and skin; Ear plugs: Protect hearing around loud machinery; Fit and care: Train staff to wear it correctly. Keep it clean and in good repair.

what-to-do-in-a-workplace-emergency.title: Responding to a workplace emergency
what-to-do-in-a-workplace-emergency.caption: Four contingency measures from the guide.
what-to-do-in-a-workplace-emergency.body:
In short: Four contingency measures from the guide.

Responding to a workplace emergency

  1. Evacuation. Move people away from the scene so it does not get worse, and on to medical care.
  2. Isolation. Separate those affected so others are not exposed and they get proper attention.
  3. Decontamination. Remove the contamination after chemical exposure where it can be controlled.
  4. Emergency personnel. Call an expert or the emergency team as early as you can.

Why it matters in theatre

Fire, a gas leak or a chemical spill in theatre needs a calm, rehearsed response.

Remember

Know your exits, alarms and who to call before an emergency.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Responding to a workplace emergency".

Evacuation: Move people away from the scene so it does not get worse, and on to medical care; Isolation: Separate those affected so others are not exposed and they get proper attention; Decontamination: Remove the contamination after chemical exposure where it can be controlled; Emergency personnel: Call an expert or the emergency team as early as you can.

emergencies-and-drills-every-theatre-wor.title: Emergencies and drills
emergencies-and-drills-every-theatre-wor.caption: The incidents and emergency procedures listed in the guide.
emergencies-and-drills-every-theatre-wor.body:
In short: The incidents and emergency procedures listed in the guide.

Emergencies and drills

  1. Fire. Know where the extinguishers are and practise the fire drill.
  2. Leaks and toxic emissions. Gas, chemical or fumes: raise the alarm and isolate.
  3. Equipment accidents. Stop the machine, make it safe and report it.
  4. Explosion. Evacuate and call emergency help.
  5. Injury to staff. Give first aid or basic life support and call for help.
  6. Structural failure. Ceilings, floors or supports: clear the area.
  7. Be prepared. Fire drills, first aid, extinguishers, basic life support, disaster planning.

Why it matters in theatre

Regular drills mean everyone in theatre knows what to do.

Remember

Practise drills. Nobody thinks well in their first emergency.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Emergencies and drills".

Fire: Know where the extinguishers are and practise the fire drill; Leaks and toxic emissions: Gas, chemical or fumes: raise the alarm and isolate; Equipment accidents: Stop the machine, make it safe and report it; Explosion: Evacuate and call emergency help; Injury to staff: Give first aid or basic life support and call for help; Structural failure: Ceilings, floors or supports: clear the area; Be prepared: Fire drills, first aid, extinguishers, basic life support, disaster planning.

your-three-rights-at-work-know-take-part.title: Your three rights at work
your-three-rights-at-work-know-take-part.caption: Three worker rights in occupational safety and health.
your-three-rights-at-work-know-take-part.body:
In short: Three worker rights in occupational safety and health.

Your three rights at work

  1. The right to know. Your employer must tell you the hazards of your job and how they are controlled, and train you.
  2. The right to take part. You can be involved in occupational health and safety, for example in a committee.
  3. The right to refuse. You can refuse work you honestly believe is unusually dangerous. You may not be punished for using these rights.

Why it matters in theatre

These rights protect theatre staff dealing with chemicals, radiation, lifting and infection risks.

Remember

You can refuse unusually dangerous work. Say so and report it.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Your three rights at work".

The right to know: Your employer must tell you the hazards of your job and how they are controlled, and train you; The right to take part: You can be involved in occupational health and safety, for example in a committee; The right to refuse: You can refuse work you honestly believe is unusually dangerous. You may not be punished for using these rights.

Study aid only. Practice varies, so follow your hospital's protocol and your supervisor's instructions.

Based on TVET CDACC, Learning Guide for Basic Competencies Level 6 (2019), rewritten as short study notes. The guide describes these rights generally. Check the Occupational Safety and Health Act 2007 for how they apply in Kenya.

duties-of-employers-and-workers-for-safe.title: Who is responsible for safety
duties-of-employers-and-workers-for-safe.caption: Employer and worker duties under the guide.
duties-of-employers-and-workers-for-safe.body:
In short: Employer and worker duties under the guide.

Who is responsible for safety

  1. Employer. Provide safe and healthy working conditions, including protection from violence, discrimination and harassment.
  2. Worker. Protect your own health and safety and that of your colleagues.
  3. Co-operate. Work with your supervisor and anyone else who has safety duties.
  4. Respect others. Never start or join in harassing another worker.
  5. Training. Employers must train workers, especially new staff, who face higher injury rates.

Why it matters in theatre

New staff in theatre need an orientation and supervision. They get hurt more often than experienced staff.

Remember

Safety is a shared duty. Everyone has a part.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Who is responsible for safety".

Employer: Provide safe and healthy working conditions, including protection from violence, discrimination and harassment; Worker: Protect your own health and safety and that of your colleagues; Co-operate: Work with your supervisor and anyone else who has safety duties; Respect others: Never start or join in harassing another worker; Training: Employers must train workers, especially new staff, who face higher injury rates.

osh-records-accident-near-miss-and-notif.title: Safety records that must be kept
osh-records-accident-near-miss-and-notif.caption: Records that support workplace safety.
osh-records-accident-near-miss-and-notif.body:
In short: Records that support workplace safety.

Safety records that must be kept

  1. Accident reports. Investigate each accident, find the underlying cause and review the report.
  2. Dangerous occurrences. Recorded in a register in the format set by the OSH regulations.
  3. Near misses. Report them too. The OSH committee keeps a register and investigates.
  4. Notifiable diseases. The OSH committee keeps a register of reported occupational disease.
  5. Training and health records. Keep records of OSH training, medical records and sick-leave notes.

Why it matters in theatre

A needle-stick or a spill that caused no harm this time still deserves a report.

Remember

Report near misses. They prevent the next injury.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Safety records that must be kept".

Accident reports: Investigate each accident, find the underlying cause and review the report; Dangerous occurrences: Recorded in a register in the format set by the OSH regulations; Near misses: Report them too. The OSH committee keeps a register and investigates; Notifiable diseases: The OSH committee keeps a register of reported occupational disease; Training and health records: Keep records of OSH training, medical records and sick-leave notes.

osh-programmes-for-health-workers.title: Occupational health programmes
osh-programmes-for-health-workers.caption: Programmes health facilities use to keep staff safe.
osh-programmes-for-health-workers.body:
In short: Programmes health facilities use to keep staff safe.

Occupational health programmes

  1. Medical surveillance. Planned, regular check-ups, including clinical examination and monitoring of biological effects.
  2. Periodic health surveillance. Regular examinations that identify groups of staff who are more vulnerable.
  3. Managing exposure. Keeping track of how much of a workplace agent has reached each worker.
  4. Induction. Every new member of staff gets orientation on safety.
  5. Audits and PPE supply. Run risk assessments and make sure good PPE is bought and available.

Why it matters in theatre

Theatre staff are exposed to infection, chemicals and radiation, so regular surveillance matters.

Remember

Health checks protect you before a problem becomes serious.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Occupational health programmes".

managing-stress-in-the-theatre-team.title: Managing stress at work
managing-stress-in-the-theatre-team.caption: Stress and how to manage it.
managing-stress-in-the-theatre-team.body:
In short: Stress and how to manage it.

Managing stress at work

  1. Set priorities. Deal with what is urgent first, using your time wisely.
  2. Check expectations. Set goals you can reach. Mistakes can teach you.
  3. Accept change. Be adaptable and build a support network of friends and family.
  4. Live healthily. Eat well, rest, exercise, pray or meditate.
  5. Workplace support. Ask for programmes that help staff cope with work stress.

Why it matters in theatre

Long lists, emergencies and long hours are part of theatre life. Managing stress protects safety and patients.

Remember

Stress builds when demands outweigh your resources. Ask for help early.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Managing stress at work".

Set priorities: Deal with what is urgent first, using your time wisely; Check expectations: Set goals you can reach. Mistakes can teach you; Accept change: Be adaptable and build a support network of friends and family; Live healthily: Eat well, rest, exercise, pray or meditate; Workplace support: Ask for programmes that help staff cope with work stress.

punctuality-and-time-consciousness-in-th.title: Punctuality and time
punctuality-and-time-consciousness-in-th.caption: Why time consciousness matters.
punctuality-and-time-consciousness-in-th.body:
In short: Why time consciousness matters.

Punctuality and time

  1. Be on time. Punctuality shows professionalism. Lateness wastes the team's time.
  2. Know your time wasters. Notice what steals your time and deal with it.
  3. Plan the day. List what has to be done and make sure it is finished on time.
  4. Benefits. Better decisions, less anxiety, better performance and better relationships.
  5. Leisure matters. Rest reduces stress and boredom and improves quality of life.

Why it matters in theatre

A late start delays every case after it.

Remember

Theatre lists wait for no one. Be ready before the case.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Punctuality and time".

Be on time: Punctuality shows professionalism. Lateness wastes the team's time; Know your time wasters: Notice what steals your time and deal with it; Plan the day: List what has to be done and make sure it is finished on time; Benefits: Better decisions, less anxiety, better performance and better relationships; Leisure matters: Rest reduces stress and boredom and improves quality of life.

how-to-set-work-priorities-in-theatre.title: Setting work priorities
how-to-set-work-priorities-in-theatre.caption: Five steps for choosing what to do first.
how-to-set-work-priorities-in-theatre.body:
In short: Five steps for choosing what to do first.

Setting work priorities

  1. List all the tasks. Write down everything that needs doing.
  2. Urgent or important?. Sort tasks by how urgent and how important they are.
  3. Weigh the value. Consider the impact on patients and colleagues.
  4. Stay flexible. Priorities can change suddenly, such as an emergency case.
  5. Know when to cut. You cannot do everything. Drop what will not get done today.

Why it matters in theatre

Theatre changes quickly. An emergency can reshuffle the whole list.

Remember

Do the urgent and important tasks first.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Setting work priorities".

safety-consciousness-in-the-theatre.title: Safety consciousness
safety-consciousness-in-the-theatre.caption: What safety consciousness means.
safety-consciousness-in-the-theatre.body:
In short: What safety consciousness means.

Safety consciousness

  1. What it is. Being aware and alert to hazards all the time.
  2. Why it matters. Most injuries happen when people stop paying attention to danger.
  3. Regular reminders. Staff need frequent safety reminders at meetings and during work.
  4. Take responsibility. Act on what you see and take precautions.
  5. Healthy workplace. Employers should build safe working into daily routine.

Why it matters in theatre

Counting, checking and speaking up are all part of a safety-conscious team.

Remember

Stay alert. Most accidents follow lost attention.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Safety consciousness".

What it is: Being aware and alert to hazards all the time; Why it matters: Most injuries happen when people stop paying attention to danger; Regular reminders: Staff need frequent safety reminders at meetings and during work; Take responsibility: Act on what you see and take precautions; Healthy workplace: Employers should build safe working into daily routine.

code-of-conduct-and-professional-integri.title: Code of conduct and integrity
code-of-conduct-and-professional-integri.caption: Conduct and integrity expected at work.
code-of-conduct-and-professional-integri.body:
In short: Conduct and integrity expected at work.

Code of conduct and integrity

  1. Know the code. Every employee must know the code of conduct and follow it.
  2. Report breaches. You also have a duty to report violations of the code.
  3. Consequences. Breaking the code can mean disciplinary action, dismissal or prosecution.
  4. Integrity. Being honest, consistent and holding to your values in every situation.
  5. Be accountable. You answer for your work and your behaviour.

Why it matters in theatre

Patients trust theatre staff with their lives. Honesty and accountability protect that trust.

Remember

Integrity means doing the right thing even when no one is watching.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Code of conduct and integrity".

Know the code: Every employee must know the code of conduct and follow it; Report breaches: You also have a duty to report violations of the code; Consequences: Breaking the code can mean disciplinary action, dismissal or prosecution; Integrity: Being honest, consistent and holding to your values in every situation; Be accountable: You answer for your work and your behaviour.

principles-of-ethics-in-healthcare-work.title: Principles of ethics
principles-of-ethics-in-healthcare-work.caption: Five ethical principles from the guide.
principles-of-ethics-in-healthcare-work.body:
In short: Five ethical principles from the guide.

Principles of ethics

  1. Truthfulness. Do not hide facts or lie to people who need to know.
  2. Confidentiality. Keep information private unless you have permission to share it.
  3. Autonomy. Respect a person's right to decide for themselves.
  4. Doing good. Everything you do should benefit the client.
  5. Justice. Treat everyone fairly and without bias.

Why it matters in theatre

They apply to every patient who comes through theatre.

Remember

Patient information stays private. Discuss it only with those who need it.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Principles of ethics".

Truthfulness: Do not hide facts or lie to people who need to know; Confidentiality: Keep information private unless you have permission to share it; Autonomy: Respect a person's right to decide for themselves; Doing good: Everything you do should benefit the client; Justice: Treat everyone fairly and without bias.

how-to-set-expectations-for-a-theatre-te.title: Team expectations
how-to-set-expectations-for-a-theatre-te.caption: Six shared team expectations.
how-to-set-expectations-for-a-theatre-te.body:
In short: Six shared team expectations.

Team expectations

  1. Respect and courtesy. Treat teammates with respect.
  2. Be flexible. Accept changes in tasks and assignments.
  3. Ask for help. Speak up when you need support.
  4. Work safely together. Safety is a shared responsibility.
  5. Be reliable. Stay motivated and dependable.
  6. Share ideas. Offer ideas that improve the team's work.

Why it matters in theatre

Surgeons, anaesthetists, nurses and technologists must work as one team.

Remember

A good team holds each other accountable, kindly.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Team expectations".

Respect and courtesy: Treat teammates with respect; Be flexible: Accept changes in tasks and assignments; Ask for help: Speak up when you need support; Work safely together: Safety is a shared responsibility; Be reliable: Stay motivated and dependable; Share ideas: Offer ideas that improve the team's work.

delegating-duties-to-team-members.title: Delegating tasks well
delegating-duties-to-team-members.caption: Guidelines for assigning duties.
delegating-duties-to-team-members.body:
In short: Guidelines for assigning duties.

Delegating tasks well

  1. Choose what to delegate. Not every task can be handed over.
  2. Set clear objectives. Make sure the person knows exactly what must be achieved.
  3. Give a timeline. Deadlines keep everyone accountable.
  4. Show respect. Make clear the person is relied on and appreciated.
  5. Match strengths. Give tasks to those who do them best.

Why it matters in theatre

Clear roles for scrub, circulating and anaesthetic teams prevent confusion.

Remember

Clear roles raise morale, efficiency and productivity.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Delegating tasks well".

Choose what to delegate: Not every task can be handed over; Set clear objectives: Make sure the person knows exactly what must be achieved; Give a timeline: Deadlines keep everyone accountable; Show respect: Make clear the person is relied on and appreciated; Match strengths: Give tasks to those who do them best.

the-communication-cycle-in-theatre.title: The communication cycle
the-communication-cycle-in-theatre.caption: The parts of the communication cycle.
the-communication-cycle-in-theatre.body:
In short: The parts of the communication cycle.

The communication cycle

  1. Sender. Starts the communication.
  2. Message. The information to be passed on.
  3. Encoding. Putting the message into words, writing or signals.
  4. Medium. How it travels: speech, writing, signals.
  5. Decoding and receiver. The receiver interprets what was sent.
  6. Feedback. The receiver responds to confirm understanding. Noise can disturb the cycle.

Why it matters in theatre

Closed-loop communication keeps instrument and swab requests accurate.

Remember

Repeat orders back. Feedback closes the loop.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "The communication cycle".

Sender: Starts the communication; Message: The information to be passed on; Encoding: Putting the message into words, writing or signals; Medium: How it travels: speech, writing, signals; Decoding and receiver: The receiver interprets what was sent; Feedback: The receiver responds to confirm understanding. Noise can disturb the cycle.

barriers-to-effective-communication.title: Barriers to communication
barriers-to-effective-communication.caption: Nine communication barriers.
barriers-to-effective-communication.body:
In short: Nine communication barriers.

Barriers to communication

  1. Physical. Noise, distance or poor equipment.
  2. Personal. Attitudes, emotions and habits.
  3. Language. Words, jargon or accents that are not understood.
  4. Status. Rank makes people hesitate to speak.
  5. Organisational structure. Information does not flow properly.
  6. Inadequate attention. Not really listening.
  7. Premature evaluation. Judging before hearing it all.
  8. Emotional evaluation. Reacting from feeling.
  9. Resistance to change. Refusing new methods.

Why it matters in theatre

Noise and hierarchy in theatre can block key messages.

Remember

Speak up whatever the rank. Clear words protect patients.

qualities-of-effective-communication.title: Effective communication
qualities-of-effective-communication.caption: Qualities of effective communication.
qualities-of-effective-communication.body:
In short: Qualities of effective communication.

Effective communication

  1. Clear. Easy to understand.
  2. Coherent. Ideas follow logically.
  3. Courteous. Polite and respectful.
  4. Complete. Contains everything the receiver needs.
  5. Focused. Stays on the point.
  6. Sensitive to emotions. Considers how people feel.
  7. Listened to keenly. The receiver pays full attention.

Why it matters in theatre

Short, complete messages prevent mistakes in theatre.

Remember

Clear, complete and courteous. Always.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Effective communication".

Clear: Easy to understand; Coherent: Ideas follow logically; Courteous: Polite and respectful; Complete: Contains everything the receiver needs; Focused: Stays on the point; Sensitive to emotions: Considers how people feel; Listened to keenly: The receiver pays full attention.

resolving-conflict-at-work-six-steps.title: Resolving conflict at work
resolving-conflict-at-work-six-steps.caption: A six-step approach to workplace conflict.
resolving-conflict-at-work-six-steps.body:
In short: A six-step approach to workplace conflict.

Resolving conflict at work

  1. Face it. Do not pretend it has not happened.
  2. Talk together. Find a time and place without interruptions.
  3. Listen carefully. Give full attention and ask for clarification.
  4. Find agreement. Look for common ground and rebuild trust.
  5. Give guidance. Agree the next steps.
  6. Forgive quickly. Let go of grudges.

Why it matters in theatre

Unresolved tension in the team puts patients at risk.

Remember

Address conflict quickly, privately and respectfully.

communication-strategies-for-a-job-inter.title: Job interview strategies
communication-strategies-for-a-job-inter.caption: Strategies from the guide for interviews.
communication-strategies-for-a-job-inter.body:
In short: Strategies from the guide for interviews.

Job interview strategies

  1. Build rapport. Smile, make eye contact, greet sincerely, use the interviewer's name.
  2. Listen more than you talk. Show real interest in the organisation and the job.
  3. Research. Learn about the employer and the industry beforehand.
  4. Prepare answers. Prepare for common questions and why you want the job.
  5. Prepare questions. Be ready for "Any questions?"
  6. Mind body language. Posture, gestures and tone of voice all communicate.
  7. Close well. End on a positive note.

Why it matters in theatre

Useful when applying for theatre posts or attachments.

Remember

First impressions count. Prepare well.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Job interview strategies".

types-of-biomedical-waste.title: Biomedical waste classes
types-of-biomedical-waste.caption: Biomedical waste is waste from health facilities and research.
types-of-biomedical-waste.body:
In short: Biomedical waste is waste from health facilities and research.

Biomedical waste classes

  1. Infectious waste. Waste that may carry infection.
  2. Sharps. Needles, blades and other items that can cut or puncture.
  3. Pharmaceutical waste. Expired or unused medicines.
  4. Chemical waste. Disinfectants, solvents and other chemicals.
  5. Pathological waste. Tissues and body parts.

Why it matters in theatre

Theatre generates every class on this card. Correct segregation protects staff and the community.

Remember

Segregate waste at the point of generation.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Biomedical waste classes".

Infectious waste: Waste that may carry infection; Sharps: Needles, blades and other items that can cut or puncture; Pharmaceutical waste: Expired or unused medicines; Chemical waste: Disinfectants, solvents and other chemicals; Pathological waste: Tissues and body parts.

steps-in-managing-solid-waste.title: Managing solid waste
steps-in-managing-solid-waste.caption: The waste management chain.
steps-in-managing-solid-waste.body:
In short: The waste management chain.

Managing solid waste

  1. Generation. Reduce, reuse and segregate at the source using coded bags and bins.
  2. Collection. Collect often to stop waste scattering.
  3. Transportation. Closed vehicles licensed by NEMA.
  4. Treatment. Recycling, composting or thermal treatment.
  5. Disposal. Sanitary landfill, covered and managed.

Why it matters in theatre

Correct segregation in theatre makes the rest of the chain safer.

Remember

Colour-coded bins only work if everyone uses them correctly.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Managing solid waste".

waste-treatment-methods.title: Waste treatment methods
waste-treatment-methods.caption: Treatment and disposal options.
waste-treatment-methods.body:
In short: Treatment and disposal options.

Waste treatment methods

  1. Recycling. Turning waste into new products, saving raw materials and reducing pollution.
  2. Composting. Controlled decomposition of biodegradable waste into fertiliser.
  3. Thermal treatment. Burning at controlled temperatures to cut volume and neutralise hazardous parts.
  4. Sanitary landfill. Buried waste with systems to collect leachate and gas.

Why it matters in theatre

Infectious waste usually needs treatment before disposal. Follow your hospital policy.

Remember

Not all waste can be recycled. Segregate correctly.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Waste treatment methods".

Recycling: Turning waste into new products, saving raw materials and reducing pollution; Composting: Controlled decomposition of biodegradable waste into fertiliser; Thermal treatment: Burning at controlled temperatures to cut volume and neutralise hazardous parts; Sanitary landfill: Buried waste with systems to collect leachate and gas.

controlling-noise-in-the-workplace.title: Controlling noise
controlling-noise-in-the-workplace.caption: Four ways to reduce noise.
controlling-noise-in-the-workplace.body:
In short: Four ways to reduce noise.

Controlling noise

  1. Source control. Reduce noise at its source or limit hours of operation.
  2. Path control. Enclose or insulate to block the sound travelling.
  3. Receiver control. Change schedules or provide earplugs.
  4. Maintenance. Well-maintained machines run more quietly.

Why it matters in theatre

Theatre equipment such as suction, drills and alarms adds up. Maintenance and PPE help.

Remember

Noise is measured in decibels. Protect your hearing.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Controlling noise".

Source control: Reduce noise at its source or limit hours of operation; Path control: Enclose or insulate to block the sound travelling; Receiver control: Change schedules or provide earplugs; Maintenance: Well-maintained machines run more quietly.

controlling-air-pollution-at-work.title: Protecting workers from air pollution
controlling-air-pollution-at-work.caption: Worker protection from air pollution.
controlling-air-pollution-at-work.body:
In short: Worker protection from air pollution.

Protecting workers from air pollution

  1. Inform workers. Tell staff about the hazards in their work area.
  2. Train them. Teach safety precautions for hazardous substances.
  3. Measure. Pollutants should be measured by an approved laboratory.
  4. Keep records. Record measurements and report to the authority.
  5. Reduce exposure. Take steps to lower exposure.

Why it matters in theatre

Anaesthetic gases and disinfectant vapours are examples.

Remember

If you cannot see the hazard, measure it.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Protecting workers from air pollution".

the-3rs-reduce-reuse-recycle-in-a-health.title: Cutting waste
the-3rs-reduce-reuse-recycle-in-a-health.caption: Ideas from the guide on reducing waste and circular economy.
the-3rs-reduce-reuse-recycle-in-a-health.body:
In short: Ideas from the guide on reducing waste and circular economy.

Cutting waste

  1. Reduce. Use less to begin with.
  2. Reuse. Use items again where it is safe to do so.
  3. Repair. Fix equipment instead of throwing it away.
  4. Recycle. Turn waste into new products.
  5. Return. Send products back to the supplier where possible.

Why it matters in theatre

Reuse only what policy allows. Single-use items and infection control rules come first.

Remember

The best waste is the waste you never create.

Check yourself

Recall the points on "Cutting waste".

protecting-data-and-patient-information.title: Protecting data
protecting-data-and-patient-information.caption: Basics of data security and privacy.
protecting-data-and-patient-information.body:
In short: Basics of data security and privacy.

Protecting data

  1. Data security. Keep data available only to those who need it.
  2. Data privacy. Decide what can be shared with third parties.
  3. Collect only what you need. Keep it safe and destroy it when no longer needed.
  4. Know the threats. Accidents, equipment failure, theft and deliberate attacks.
  5. Weakest link. Attackers go around security to the weakest point, often people.

Why it matters in theatre

Theatre registers and patient records contain sensitive information.

Remember

Patient information is confidential.

Recall the points on "Protecting data".
